iberia.description: Ferdinand VI’s Spain, steered by the Marqués de la Ensenada, rebuilds fleets and finances under Bourbon centralism; the 1750 Treaty of Madrid redraws the Spanish–Portuguese line in South America. Portugal, rich on Brazilian gold, gets a new king (Joseph I, 1750) and a new strongman, the future Marquis of Pombal—five years before the Lisbon earthquake. Genetics: continuity.

britain.description: Culloden (1746) ends the last Jacobite rising and the clan order of the Highlands. Britain’s parliamentary, debt-financed state pays for a navy that outguns France; Ireland is ruled by a Protestant Ascendancy under the Penal Laws. Hume, Smith and the Scottish Enlightenment flourish; Methodist field preaching spreads. Genetics: continuity.

france.description: Louis XV’s France is Europe’s most populous kingdom and its cultural capital: Montesquieu’s Spirit of the Laws (1748) and the first volume of the Encyclopédie (1751) come out of Paris. The monarchy fights Jansenists and parlements at home and Britain overseas. Genetics: continuity.

central.description: Frederick II’s seizure of Silesia (1740) sets Prussia against Austria for a generation. Maria Theresa survives the War of the Austrian Succession, wins Hungarian support at the 1741 Diet, and then reforms taxation and the army (Haugwitz, 1749). The Holy Roman Empire endures as a legal frame of hundreds of states; Bach dies in Leipzig in 1750. Genetics: continuity plus Danube resettlement.

scandinavia.description: Sweden, stripped of its Baltic empire in 1721, is ruled by its Riksdag parties (Hats and Caps) and loses more of Finland to Russia in 1743. Denmark–Norway is an absolute monarchy at peace, building Copenhagen’s Frederiksstaden. Linnaeus classifies the living world from Uppsala. Genetics: continuity.

italy.description: The 1748 peace freezes Italy: Bourbons in Naples–Sicily and Parma, Habsburgs in Milan, the Habsburg-Lorraine emperor in Tuscany, Savoy in Piedmont–Sardinia, with Venice, Genoa and the Papal States as old republics and a church state. Benedict XIV is a scholar-pope; Herculaneum and Pompeii are being dug up. Genetics: continuity.

balkans.description: After the 1739 Peace of Belgrade the Danube–Sava line is the border between Ottoman and Habsburg Europe. Wallachia and Moldavia are ruled by Phanariot Greek princes appointed from Istanbul; Constantine Mavrocordatos abolishes serfdom there in the 1740s. Serbs have fled north to the Habsburg Military Frontier. Genetics: continuity with frontier migration.

eastern.description: Empress Elizabeth’s Russia holds the Baltic provinces and the Hetmanate of left-bank Ukraine (restored under Kyrylo Rozumovsky in 1750). Poland–Lithuania, under the Saxon king Augustus III, is a large but weak noble republic. The Crimean Khanate and the Ottomans still hold the Black Sea coast. Genetics: continuity.

GBR.art: Hogarth’s moral series, Canaletto’s London views, Allan Ramsay’s portraits; Handel’s Messiah (1742) and Music for the Royal Fireworks (1749).
GBR.ideas: Mixed constitution, rule of Parliament, public credit and commercial empire.

images.alt: An Incident in the Rebellion of 1745 (Culloden) — David Morier
images.caption: An Incident in the Rebellion of 1745 (Culloden) — David Morier

GBR.literature: Fielding’s Tom Jones (1749), Richardson’s Clarissa (1748) and Samuel Johnson’s Dictionary (1755) shape the English novel and language.
GBR.philosophy: David Hume’s Enquiry concerning Human Understanding (1748); Francis Hutcheson and Adam Smith teach moral philosophy in Glasgow.
GBR.science: John Harrison’s marine timekeepers; James Bradley as Astronomer Royal; the 1752 switch to the Gregorian calendar.
GBR.story: In April 1746 the Duke of Cumberland’s army destroys Charles Edward Stuart’s Highlanders at Culloden. Within a few years the Highlands are disarmed, the old heritable jurisdictions abolished, and Britain turns its energy to the sea and the war for empire with France.

IRL.art: Georgian Dublin architecture; harp music after Turlough O’Carolan (d. 1738).
IRL.literature: Jonathan Swift (d. 1745) leaves Gulliver’s Travels and A Modest Proposal; Gaelic poets lament the fall of the old order.
IRL.philosophy: George Berkeley, Bishop of Cloyne, and his immaterialism.
IRL.science: The Dublin Society (founded 1731) promotes agriculture and industry.
IRL.story: Handel’s Messiah has its first performance in Dublin in April 1742. The city is building squares and a parliament house worthy of a capital, while most Irish speakers outside it rent land they cannot own.

FRA.art: Boucher, Chardin, Maurice-Quentin de La Tour; the Place Louis XV (today’s Place de la Concorde) planned in the 1750s.
FRA.literature: Voltaire’s Siècle de Louis XIV (1751); Rousseau’s Discourse on the Sciences and Arts (1750); Montesquieu’s The Spirit of the Laws (1748).
FRA.science: Buffon’s Histoire naturelle (from 1749); Maupertuis’s Lapland expedition settled the Earth’s shape.
FRA.story: In 1751 Diderot and d’Alembert publish the first volume of the Encyclopédie. Within a year the royal council suppresses the first two volumes, and publication continues anyway—a sign of how far the reading public has grown beyond the court’s control.

ESP.art: The new Royal Palace of Madrid (from 1738); Domenico Scarlatti’s keyboard sonatas written in Madrid.
ESP.ideas: Reform from above: the Ensenada cadastre for a single tax.

images.alt: Charles III, Ferdinand’s half-brother, then King of Naples
images.caption: Charles III, Ferdinand’s half-brother, then King of Naples

images.alt: Farinelli and friends — Jacopo Amigoni, c. 1750–52
images.caption: Farinelli and friends — Jacopo Amigoni, c. 1750–52

ESP.literature: Benito Jerónimo Feijoo’s Teatro crítico universal and Cartas eruditas attack superstition.
ESP.science: Jorge Juan and Antonio de Ulloa, veterans of the French geodesic mission to Peru; new naval arsenals.
ESP.story: Farinelli, the most famous singer in Europe, spends two decades at the Spanish court singing to calm Philip V and then directing opera for Ferdinand VI—an Italian voice at the heart of a French dynasty ruling Spain.

PRT.art: The palace-convent of Mafra; azulejo tile panels.
PRT.literature: Luís António Verney’s O Verdadeiro Método de Estudar (1746) attacks Jesuit schooling.
PRT.science: The rebuilt Lisbon Baixa uses the gaiola, an anti-seismic timber cage.
PRT.story: On 1 November 1755 an earthquake, fire and tsunami destroy much of Lisbon. Pombal’s reply—bury the dead, feed the living—and the rebuilding of the Baixa on a grid with earthquake-resistant frames make him the master of the state.

images.alt: Johan de Witt, symbol of the old republican party
images.caption: Johan de Witt, symbol of the old republican party

images.alt: Spinoza, whose Dutch toleration the century inherited
images.caption: Spinoza, whose Dutch toleration the century inherited

NLD.literature: Dutch presses print what Paris bans: Amsterdam and Leiden publish much of the French Enlightenment.
NLD.philosophy: Hemsterhuis later; the republic of letters’ printing house.
NLD.science: Pieter van Musschenbroek at Leiden builds the Leyden jar (1745–46).
NLD.story: In 1747 French troops cross into Dutch Flanders and the provinces, in panic, make William IV hereditary stadtholder of all seven—ending the republic’s second stadtholderless period.

BEL.art: Grand Place guildhouses rebuilt after 1695; Rubens’s legacy in the churches.

images.alt: Rubens’s Descent from the Cross — the Flemish inheritance
images.caption: Rubens’s Descent from the Cross — the Flemish inheritance

BEL.literature: French-language court culture in Brussels; Flemish devotional print.
BEL.story: After Fontenoy Marshal de Saxe takes the Netherlands fortress by fortress; at the peace of 1748 France hands them all back, a decision Parisians mocked as ‘bête comme la paix’—stupid as the peace.

DEU.art: Sanssouci rococo; Tiepolo’s Würzburg Residenz frescoes (1750–53); J. S. Bach dies in Leipzig in 1750.
DEU.ideas: Enlightened absolutism: ‘first servant of the state’.
DEU.literature: Klopstock begins Der Messias (1748); Gottsched and Lessing reform German drama.
DEU.philosophy: Christian Wolff’s rationalism dominates German universities; Kant begins teaching in Königsberg in 1755.
DEU.science: Leonhard Euler at the Berlin Academy (1741–66); University of Göttingen (1737).
DEU.story: Frederick builds Sanssouci (1745–47) as a retreat ‘without care’, plays the flute for guests, invites Voltaire (1750–53), and keeps the largest army per head in Europe.

AUT.art: Schönbrunn rebuilt for Maria Theresa; Bellotto’s Vienna views (1758–61); Gluck’s early operas.

images.alt: Joseph II, heir to the reforms
images.caption: Joseph II, heir to the reforms

AUT.literature: Metastasio, imperial court poet in Vienna, writes the opera librettos the whole continent sets to music.
AUT.philosophy: Catholic Enlightenment reform under Gerard van Swieten.
AUT.science: Van Swieten reforms medical teaching in Vienna.
AUT.story: In 1756 Kaunitz achieves the ‘Diplomatic Revolution’: Austria allies with its old enemy France, while Britain sides with Prussia—a reversal meant to win Silesia back.

CZE.art: Kilian Ignaz Dientzenhofer’s churches, including St Nicholas in Prague’s Lesser Town.
CZE.ideas: Bohemian estates losing ground to central government.

images.alt: White Mountain (1620), the defeat that shaped Habsburg Bohemia
images.caption: White Mountain (1620), the defeat that shaped Habsburg Bohemia

images.alt: Maria Theresa, crowned Queen of Bohemia in 1743
images.caption: Maria Theresa, crowned Queen of Bohemia in 1743

CZE.literature: Czech literature survives in devotional and popular print.
CZE.science: Prokop Diviš experiments with a lightning conductor (1754).
CZE.story: In 1741 the Elector of Bavaria is crowned King of Bohemia in Prague; two years later Maria Theresa takes the crown back and the Bohemian Court Chancellery is soon merged into Vienna’s central administration (1749).

images.alt: Siege of Buda (1686), start of the reconquest
images.caption: Siege of Buda (1686), start of the reconquest

HUN.literature: Latin scholarship (Mátyás Bél’s survey of Hungary) and Hungarian verse.
HUN.story: At the Pressburg Diet of 1741 the Hungarian nobles answer Maria Theresa’s plea with ‘vitam et sanguinem’—our life and blood—and raise the troops that save her throne.

CHE.literature: Albrecht von Haller’s poem Die Alpen (1729); Bodmer and Breitinger in Zurich.
CHE.story: Jean-Jacques Rousseau, ‘citizen of Geneva’, wins the Dijon academy prize in 1750 by arguing that the arts and sciences have corrupted morals—fame begins with a Swiss republican scolding Paris.

ITA.art: Tiepolo, Canaletto, Piranesi’s Roman views; the Trevi Fountain (completed 1762); Caserta palace (from 1752).
ITA.ideas: Reforming ministers in Naples, Milan and Tuscany.
ITA.literature: Goldoni’s comedies in Venice; Metastasio’s librettos.
ITA.philosophy: Giambattista Vico’s New Science (final edition 1744); Muratori.
ITA.science: Laura Bassi, professor of physics at Bologna; Agnesi’s calculus textbook (1748).
ITA.story: Excavations begun at Herculaneum (1738) and Pompeii (1748) under Charles of Bourbon feed a European craze for antiquity that will become neoclassicism.

POL.art: Sarmatian coffin portraits; Saxon Palace in Warsaw.

images.alt: Jan III Sobieski, the Commonwealth’s last great warrior king
images.caption: Jan III Sobieski, the Commonwealth’s last great warrior king

POL.literature: Stanisław Konarski’s On the Means of Effective Counsel (1760–63) attacks the veto.
POL.story: Between 1736 and 1763 almost every Sejm is broken by a single deputy’s veto. The Załuski brothers open one of Europe’s first public libraries in Warsaw (1747) while the state cannot pass a budget.

LTU.literature: Polish-language noble culture; Lithuanian in catechisms and hymnals.
LTU.story: Vilnius rebuilds its churches after the great fires of the 1740s in a late baroque that gives the city its skyline; in the same streets the Vilna Gaon becomes the leading rabbinic scholar of his age.

UKR.art: Rastrelli’s St Andrew’s Church in Kyiv (1747–54).

images.alt: Bakhchisaray, seat of the Crimean khans
images.caption: Bakhchisaray, seat of the Crimean khans

UKR.story: Kyrylo Rozumovsky, brother of Empress Elizabeth’s favourite, is elected hetman in 1750 at twenty-two, after the office had been vacant since 1734. He rules from Hlukhiv until Catherine II abolishes the hetmanate in 1764.

RUS.art: Rastrelli’s Winter Palace (1754–62), Smolny Convent and Catherine Palace.
RUS.ideas: Petrine state, noble service and serfdom.

images.alt: Peter the Great, the founder of the empire
images.caption: Peter the Great, the founder of the empire

RUS.literature: Lomonosov’s odes and Russian Grammar (1755); Sumarokov’s tragedies.
RUS.story: In 1755 Mikhail Lomonosov, a fisherman’s son from the White Sea, and Ivan Shuvalov found Moscow University. Lomonosov also writes the first scientific Russian grammar.

SWE.art: Drottningholm palace theatre (1766); Carl Hårleman’s interiors.
SWE.literature: Olof von Dalin’s weekly Then Swänska Argus.
SWE.story: Carl Linnaeus publishes Species Plantarum in 1753, giving every plant a two-part name and sending his ‘apostles’ around the world to collect.

images.alt: Helsinki (cathedral of 1852) — the city Sveaborg was built to protect
images.caption: Helsinki (cathedral of 1852) — the city Sveaborg was built to protect

FIN.literature: Finnish in sermons and hymns; Swedish in print.
FIN.science: Pehr Kalm, Linnaeus’s pupil, travels to North America (1748–51).
FIN.story: From 1748 Augustin Ehrensvärd builds the sea fortress of Sveaborg (Suomenlinna) off Helsinki to keep the Russian fleet out of Finland.

DNK.story: For the monarchy’s 300th jubilee in 1749 Frederick V lays out Frederiksstaden, a new district around four palaces at Amalienborg.

images.alt: Røros church (1784), in the copper town
images.caption: Røros church (1784), in the copper town

NOR.story: The Strömstad treaty of 1751 fixes the long Norwegian–Swedish border and adds the Lapp Codicil, protecting Sámi reindeer herders’ right to cross it.

TUR.art: Nuruosmaniye Mosque; Ahmed III’s fountain at the Topkapı gate.
TUR.ideas: Ottoman order and military reform (Bonneval Pasha).
TUR.story: The Nuruosmaniye Mosque (1748–55) is the first imperial mosque built in the Ottoman baroque—a style borrowed from Europe at the moment the empire stops losing to it.

images.alt: The Parthenon, damaged in 1687, under Ottoman rule
images.caption: The Parthenon, damaged in 1687, under Ottoman rule

images.alt: Ottoman Iznik tiles — the imperial frame of Greek life
images.caption: Ottoman Iznik tiles — the imperial frame of Greek life

GRC.literature: Greek religious and scholarly print from Venice.
GRC.story: In 1749 the Athonite Academy is founded on Mount Athos; under Eugenios Voulgaris (from 1753) it teaches Locke and Newton to Orthodox students.

ROU.ideas: Phanariot reform; Romanian estate claims in Transylvania.

images.alt: Mahmud I, suzerain of the Principalities
images.caption: Mahmud I, suzerain of the Principalities

ROU.literature: Bishop Inochentie Micu-Klein argues for Transylvanian Romanians’ rights.
ROU.philosophy: Princely academies at Bucharest and Iași.
ROU.story: Constantine Mavrocordatos abolishes serfdom in Wallachia (1746) and Moldavia (1749), turning serfs into peasants owing fixed labour dues—a reform decades before Vienna’s.

images.alt: Belgrade fortress (Kalemegdan), rebuilt by Austria and returned in 1739
images.caption: Belgrade fortress (Kalemegdan), rebuilt by Austria and returned in 1739

images.alt: Serbian Orthodoxy (modern Church of Saint Sava, Belgrade)
images.caption: Serbian Orthodoxy (modern Church of Saint Sava, Belgrade)

SRB.literature: Church Slavonic in Russian redaction; Zaharija Orfelin later.
SRB.science: Learning moves north: Serbian schools at Sremski Karlovci (gymnasium founded 1791) grow from the church culture of the Habsburg Serbs.
SRB.story: In 1737–39 Patriarch Arsenije IV leads Serbs north across the Danube; the Metropolitanate of Karlovci becomes the centre of Serbian culture for a century.
